languages.label: Go
languages.tagline: Slices, interfaces, goroutines, and the zero values in between.

misconceptions.description: Believing append always copies, so the returned slice never shares backing storage with the original and writes through one cannot be seen through the other.
Believing a slice is passed by reference, so append inside a function changes the caller's length, rather than the header being copied by value.
Believing s[1:3] copies elements into a new array instead of creating a view over the same backing array.
Believing len and cap are the same thing, so make([]int, 5) and make([]int, 0, 5) are interchangeable.
Believing a nil slice must be initialised before use, rather than being a valid empty slice that supports len, range and append.
Believing you can assign into a nil map the way you can append to a nil slice, instead of it panicking without make.
Believing reading an absent map key panics or returns nil, rather than yielding the value type's zero value.
Believing map iteration follows insertion order or sorted key order, rather than being deliberately randomised.
Believing you can assign to a field of a struct value stored in a map (m[k].f = v) without the map holding a pointer.
Believing arrays and slices are the same, so [3]int and []int are interchangeable and arrays are passed by reference.
Believing the range value variable aliases the element, so mutating it or taking its address modifies the collection.
Believing the ranged expression and its length are re-evaluated each iteration, so appending inside the loop extends it.
Assuming (or in modern Go, still fearing) that goroutines and closures capture one shared loop variable, misjudging per-iteration scoping rules.
Believing defer runs at the end of the enclosing block or loop iteration rather than when the surrounding function returns.
Believing deferred call arguments and the receiver are evaluated when the deferred call runs, not at the point of the defer statement.
Believing a deferred function cannot alter the returned value, overlooking that it can modify named result parameters after return.
Believing go f() waits for f to finish, or that main waits for running goroutines before exiting.
Believing a send on an unbuffered channel returns immediately and buffers one value, rather than blocking until a receiver is ready.
Believing receives on a closed channel block or panic, rather than returning the zero value immediately with ok == false.
Believing every channel must be closed to avoid leaks, or that the receiver may close a channel, rather than close signalling no more sends.
Believing operations on a nil channel panic or succeed, instead of blocking forever and thus disabling a select case.
Believing select evaluates cases top to bottom and picks the first listed ready case, rather than choosing uniformly at random among ready cases.
Believing wg.Add may be called inside the spawned goroutine, or that passing a WaitGroup by value still coordinates correctly.
Believing a struct containing a sync.Mutex can be copied or passed by value and still provide mutual exclusion.
Believing that using channels or goroutines anywhere makes all shared-variable access safe, so no mutex or atomic is ever needed.
Believing an interface holding a typed nil pointer compares equal to nil, so err != nil is false when a nil *MyError is returned.
Believing a type must explicitly declare that it implements an interface, rather than satisfaction being structural and implicit.
Believing a value of type T satisfies an interface whose methods have pointer receivers, ignoring addressability and method-set rules.
Believing a method with a value receiver can mutate the original struct, instead of operating on a copy.
Believing struct embedding is subclassing with virtual dispatch, so the outer type's method overrides calls made from the embedded type's methods.
Believing s[i] yields a one-character string or a rune, rather than a byte, and that len(s) counts characters rather than bytes.
Believing a string can be modified in place via s[i] = 'x', rather than being immutable and requiring a []byte or []rune conversion.
Believing repeated s += x in a loop mutates in place at no cost, rather than allocating a new string each time where a Builder is preferable.
Believing Go implicitly converts between numeric types, so int and int64 or int and float64 can be mixed in an expression without a conversion.
Believing 3/2 produces 1.5, rather than integer division truncating toward zero when both operands are integers.
Confusing T(x) conversion with x.(T) type assertion, expecting one to do the other's runtime interface check.
Believing panic/recover is Go's normal error mechanism and that a panic in one goroutine can be recovered by another or by the caller's recover.
Believing wrapped errors can be matched with == or by comparing message strings, rather than with errors.Is and errors.As.
Believing visibility is controlled by keywords or file layout rather than identifier capitalisation, and that unexported fields marshal to JSON.
Believing := always assigns to the existing outer variable, missing that in a new scope it declares and shadows a fresh variable.

languages.label: Ruby
languages.tagline: Blocks, objects, and the dynamic behavior underneath.

misconceptions.description: Believing 0, "", [] and {} are falsy in Ruby, as in C or JavaScript; only false and nil are falsy.
Believing nil == false is true, or that nil and false are interchangeable values rather than distinct objects.
Believing the ! suffix is enforced by Ruby to mean in-place mutation, rather than being a naming convention for a more surprising or dangerous variant.
Believing mutating methods like String#strip!, Array#uniq! or #sort! always return the receiver, when they return nil if no change was made.
Believing `b = a` copies the object, so mutating b through a shared reference (e.g. b << x) will not affect a.
Believing dup or clone performs a deep copy, so nested objects inside the copy are independent of the original.
Believing freeze makes an object deeply immutable, rather than only preventing changes to the object's own state.
Believing default argument expressions are evaluated once at definition time, rather than on each call where the argument is omitted.
Believing Hash.new([]) gives each missing key its own fresh array, when all misses share one object that is never stored in the hash.
Believing hash[:missing] raises an error like fetch does, instead of returning nil or the hash's default.
Believing a method needs an explicit `return` to produce a value, rather than returning the value of its last evaluated expression.
Believing `return` inside a block returns only from the block, when it returns from the enclosing method; `next` is what exits a block.
Believing each returns an array of the block's results like map, rather than returning the original collection.
Believing map, select, reject or sort modify the receiver in place instead of returning a new collection.
Believing procs and lambdas behave identically, missing that lambdas check arity strictly and return only from themselves.
Believing a method must declare an explicit &block parameter before it can yield to a given block.
Believing single-quoted strings interpolate #{} and process escapes like \n the same way double-quoted strings do.
Believing "a" + 1 or "5" + 5 coerces automatically, rather than raising TypeError and needing to_s or to_i.
Believing String#to_i raises on non-numeric input, when "abc".to_i returns 0 and "12abc".to_i returns 12; Integer() is the strict form.
Believing 7 / 2 yields 3.5, rather than integer division truncating toward negative infinity to give 3.
Believing floating point arithmetic is exact, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to true.
Believing :name and "name" are the same object or interchangeable as hash keys, when they are distinct and not equal.
Believing ==, eql? and equal? all test the same thing, rather than value equality, type-strict equality, and object identity.
Believing === is a stricter equality operator as in JavaScript, rather than case-subsumption (class membership, regexp match, range inclusion).
Believing case/when falls through to the next branch without a break, as in C-style switch statements.
Believing `and`/`or` are exact synonyms for &&/||, missing that their much lower precedence changes how assignments parse.
Believing x ||= value leaves an existing false or nil value alone, when ||= overwrites any falsy value.
Believing &. guards against every error or against NoMethodError generally, when it only skips the call when the receiver is nil.
Believing local variables assigned inside a method, block, or class body are visible in enclosing or sibling scopes.
Believing reading an undefined instance variable raises an error, rather than quietly returning nil.
Believing a bare `name = x` inside an instance method calls the attr_writer, when it creates a local variable; self.name = x is required.
Believing private methods are invisible to subclasses or that private restricts by class rather than by receiver syntax.
Believing @@variables are per-subclass, when they are shared across the whole class hierarchy.
Believing self inside a class body refers to a future instance, rather than to the class object itself.
Believing include gives true multiple inheritance with unordered lookup, rather than inserting modules into a defined ancestor chain.
Believing to_s and inspect produce identical output, so puts and p display objects the same way.
Believing puts returns the printed string (and that p and puts return the same thing), when puts returns nil and p returns its argument.
Believing a bare `rescue` catches every exception, when it only catches StandardError and its descendants.
Believing code in ensure never runs after a return, or conversely that raising in ensure is harmless to the original exception.
Believing (1..5) excludes 5 like a half-open range in other languages, or that (1...5) includes it.

languages.label: Rails
languages.tagline: ActiveRecord, conventions, and what the framework does for you.

misconceptions.description: Believing `where` returns an Array of records immediately, rather than a lazy ActiveRecord::Relation that only queries the database when enumerated, counted, or inspected.
Believing `find`, `find_by`, and `where(...).first` behave identically — not realising `find` raises RecordNotFound on a missing id while `find_by` returns nil.
Believing `save` and `update` raise an exception when validations fail, instead of returning false; only the bang versions (`save!`, `update!`) raise.
Believing `record.errors` is populated without running validations — not realising `valid?` (or a save attempt) must run first to refresh the errors object.
Believing `update_attribute` runs validations like `update` does, when it skips validations (though it does run callbacks and touches updated_at).
Believing `update_column`/`update_columns` run validations and callbacks and bump updated_at, when they write straight to the database, skipping all of them.
Believing `validates_uniqueness_of` guarantees uniqueness, when it is a read-then-write check subject to races and requires a database unique index for real safety.
Believing `validates :x, presence: true` only rejects nil, when it rejects any blank value including empty strings, whitespace, and empty arrays — and that `false` passes presence.
Believing request params arrive as integers, booleans, or dates; in fact query and form params are strings (or hashes/arrays of strings) until explicitly cast.
Believing `permit` validates or sanitises values, when it only whitelists which keys may be mass-assigned; it performs no type checking or escaping.
Confusing `params.require(:user)` with `params.permit(:user)` — thinking `require` whitelists attributes or that `permit` raises when a key is missing.
Believing `redirect_to` or `render` immediately returns from the controller action, when execution continues and a second render/redirect raises DoubleRenderError.
Believing `render :edit` changes the browser URL like a redirect, when it only renders a template in the current request without a new HTTP round trip.
Believing `includes` and `joins` are interchangeable — not realising `joins` builds an INNER JOIN for filtering while `includes` preloads associations to avoid N+1.
Believing that looping over records and calling an association inside the loop issues one query, rather than one query per record (the N+1 problem).
Believing `count`, `size`, and `length` on a relation or association are identical, ignoring that `count` always queries, `length` loads all records, and `size` depends on load state.
Believing `pluck` returns model objects like `select` does, when it returns raw column values as an array and bypasses model instantiation and methods.
Believing `default_scope` only affects explicit queries, when it also leaks into associations, `new` defaults, and `unscoped` workarounds, making it hard to opt out of.
Believing a scope body may be a plain expression, when a non-lambda body (e.g. `where('created_at > ?', Time.now)`) is evaluated once at class load and freezes the value.
Believing the foreign key lives on the `has_many` side — not realising the table declaring `belongs_to` is the one that holds the `*_id` column.
Believing `belongs_to` is optional by default; in modern Rails it adds a presence validation unless `optional: true` is given.
Believing associated records are deleted automatically when a parent is destroyed, when nothing happens without `dependent: :destroy`/`:delete_all` or a database-level cascade.
Believing `delete`/`delete_all` run destroy callbacks and `dependent` options like `destroy`/`destroy_all`, when they issue raw DELETE statements and skip model logic.
Believing `has_many :through` works without the intermediate association or model, or confusing it with `has_and_belongs_to_many`, which has no join model at all.
Believing `Model.new` or building through an association writes to the database, when only `create`/`save` persist and `new` leaves the record unpersisted.
Believing `parent.children.build` saves at once, or that `parent.children.create` on an unsaved parent persists — ignoring how autosave defers child writes.
Believing `after_save`/`after_create` run outside the transaction so external jobs and emails see committed data; that requires `after_commit`.
Believing returning `false` from a before_* callback cancels the operation, when modern Rails requires `throw :abort` to halt the callback chain.
Believing a transaction rolls back when a block returns false or a save fails, when rollback requires a raised exception (or `raise ActiveRecord::Rollback`).
Believing editing an already-run migration changes the schema on the next `db:migrate`, when Rails tracks applied versions and skips them; a new migration or rollback is needed.
Believing models read columns from migration files, when the authoritative source is the database (and `schema.rb`), so a forgotten `db:migrate` leaves methods missing.
Believing each database column needs an `attr_accessor` or explicit attribute declaration, when ActiveRecord defines accessors from the table schema automatically.
Misreading `resources :posts`: believing it creates no show/edit routes, or that route order is irrelevant, when the first matching route wins and member/collection blocks matter.
Believing `post_path` and `post_url` are interchangeable, or that a named helper works without the matching route — ignoring that `_url` includes the host and is needed in emails.
Believing controller instance variables or memoised class-level state persist across requests, when each request gets a fresh controller instance and class state is shared unsafely.
Believing local variables from a controller action or from one partial are visible in views and other partials, when only instance variables and explicit `locals:` are passed.
Believing `html_safe` sanitises user input, when it merely marks a string as trusted and disables escaping, opening an XSS hole; `sanitize` is the sanitiser.
Believing CSRF tokens are unnecessary for JavaScript or API-style requests from the app's own pages, so disabling `protect_from_forgery` is a harmless fix for 422 errors.
Believing behaviour seen in development carries over to production, ignoring differences in eager loading, class reloading, caching, asset compilation, and error reporting.
Believing `Time.now`/`Date.today` respect the application time zone, when zone-aware code needs `Time.current`/`Time.zone.now`/`Date.current`.
